summary:
Will Bond opens by framing the scale of software engineering at Uber: thousands of engineers, hundreds of teams, twelve sites, six language-specific monorepos. PR volume and size have grown over 24 months, pushing first-time-to-review from three hours (2024) to nine hours (2026) and making code review the bottleneck. Uber chose to build uReview in-house because most vendors do not support Phabricator (their current system, while they migrate to GitHub) and because they want agents and humans reviewed under identical rules in the inner loop. Additional drivers include distributed team ownership of rules, risk/complexity-aware routing, and consistent security and compliance coverage.

Bond sketches the architecture: GitHub, Phabricator, and the agent loop feed a uReview service that routes requests, dispatches to multiple generators tuned for different cost and performance tradeoffs, and post-processes output by rating, categorizing, filtering, and deduplicating comments so engineers see only high-confidence, actionable ones.

Ameya Ketkar then describes evolution via observability and evaluation. The earliest version was a single per-file logic-check prompt with a dispatcher, measured only by cost, NPS surveys, Google Forms, and Slack support, producing scattered quality-to-cost ratios. Improvements came from reply sentiment, address rate, and agent trajectory, enabling tuning of runtime, performance, and turn-wasting guardrails. A key learning: models confidently assert wrong reviews, so team-specific style guides and anti-patterns must be embedded.

Ketkar covers deep team customization: per-file logic reviewers, monorepo-specific deep reviewers, AI linters as few-shot deterministic rule systems, and custom agents tied to team knowledge bases and past PRs. Authoring skills was easy; running them cheaply and consistently at scale was hard, requiring Uber's ownership model, co-located customizations, deterministic routing, and surfaced observability.

Bond closes on inner- versus outer-loop tradeoffs. Rather than killing the outer loop, uReview expands it: agents take over implementation details and nit-level review while human engineers focus on architecture, domain expertise, and product thinking, guiding the agentic system instead of policing every line.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Uber's first-time-to-review grew from 3 hours (2024) to 9 hours (2026), turning code review into a systemic bottleneck across six monorepos and hundreds of teams.
uReview was built in-house mainly because vendors don't support Phabricator and Uber wants agents and humans reviewed by the same rules in the inner loop.
Architecture routes requests through multiple cost/performance-tuned generators, then deduplicates and filters output.
Sentiment, address rate, and agent trajectory data moved most PRs into a high-quality/low-cost quadrant, replacing the cost/NPS/Google-Forms baseline.
Models assert bad reviews with full confidence, so team-specific style guides, anti-patterns, and turn-wasting guardrails must be embedded in the agent.

sections.title: Context and motivation
sections.summary: Will Bond sets the scene: thousands of engineers across hundreds of teams, twelve sites, and six language-specific monorepos. PR volume and size have grown over 24 months, pushing first-time-to-review from three hours (2024) to nine hours (2026), making code review the bottleneck.

sections.title: Why build rather than buy
sections.summary: Uber built uReview in-house because most vendors don't support Phabricator (which they still use while migrating to GitHub), they want agents reviewed under the same rules as humans in the inner loop, they need distributed team ownership of rules, risk/complexity-aware routing, and consistent security/compliance coverage.

sections.title: uReview architecture overview
sections.summary: GitHub, Phabricator, and the agent loop feed a uReview service that routes requests to multiple cost/performance-tuned generators (including third-party comparisons), then post-processes output by rating, categorizing, filtering, and deduplicating comments so engineers see only high-confidence, actionable ones.

sections.title: Humble beginnings and weak observability
sections.summary: Ameya Ketkar describes the earliest uReview as a single per-file logic-check prompt with a dispatcher, measured only by cost, NPS surveys, Google Forms, and Slack support, producing scattered quality-to-cost ratios.

sections.title: Adding sentiment, address rate, and trajectory
sections.summary: Reply sentiment classification surfaced fixable bug classes; tracking address rate and agent trajectory (tool calls and reasoning) enabled tuning of runtime, performance, and guardrails. A key learning: models confidently assert wrong reviews, so team-specific style guides, anti-patterns, and turn-wasting guardrails must be embedded.

sections.title: Team customization stack
sections.summary: General per-file logic reviewers, monorepo-specific multi-file deep reviewers, AI linters as few-shot deterministic rule systems, and custom agents linked to team knowledge bases and past PRs. Authoring skills was easy; running them cheaply and consistently at scale was hard, requiring piggybacking on Uber's ownership model, co-locating customizations, deterministic routing, and surfacing observability back to teams.

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: uReview posts ~25,000 comments a week; ~10% get feedback; ~4% of PRs get negative feedback; ~67% overall address rate; ~75% of high-severity issues addressed; 60% cost reduction and ~70% quality/accuracy improvement vs naive baseline.

sections.title: Inner vs outer loop in the agentic SDLC
sections.summary: Bond explains that with humans less involved in authoring code, inner-loop accuracy must rise to avoid agent cavitation. Agents tolerate nit-fix volume that frustrates humans, and reduced human feedback will require new tuning signals.

sections.title: Expanding the outer loop rather than killing it
sections.summary: Bond argues that as software engineering moves to an agentic model, the industry is coalescing on expanding the outer loop rather than removing humans. Agents take over implementation details and review, while human engineers move up a layer to focus on architecture, domain expertise, and product thinking, guiding the system.

limitations: Most third-party code review vendors do not support Phabricator
Models do not signal when wrong and assert bad reviews with full confidence
Agent quality degrades if allowed to waste turns outside the required review window
Inner-loop inaccuracy can cause agent cavitation (fix→re-review→re-fix loops)
Engineers get frustrated fixing large numbers of nit-level comments that agents tolerate
Humans are exiting the inner loop, reducing the natural-feedback signal used for tuning
Killing the outer loop risks quality degradation and code slop
